title: Pick the Smartest Method
goal: I can choose the best method for a multiplication problem and find the mistake in someone's work.

card.desc: Bailey proves the week: she picks the optimal method (basic fact, break apart, or area model), hunts for blunders in other people's work (lost zeros, wrong facts, missing boxes, lost count) and solves harder word problems. This targets her habit of grabbing the most complicated method and losing track.

win: You picked the right tool and caught the blunders. That is a triumphant week!

slides.title: Pick the Smartest Method: On Your Own
slides.text: In class you picked the best tool and hunted blunders. Now prove it on your own. Keep paper and a pencil next to you.

slides.title: Explain it out loud
slides.text: Say these to a grown-up, or say them out loud to yourself.
prompts: How do you choose between a fact, break apart and an area model?
Name the four blunders. Which one do you need to watch for?
Was a choice Hiccup made this week deliberate? Tell what happened.

slides.title: Review your words
slides.text: Say the meaning out loud first. Then flip the card to check yourself.

words.meaning: A way of doing something, step by step.
words.example: The area model is my method for 238 × 7.

words.meaning: The best possible choice for the job.
words.example: For 9 × 7, the optimal method is just knowing the fact.

words.meaning: Correct and based on good reasons.
words.example: Hiccup's answer is valid: every box is right.
Writing 42 instead of 420 in the 60 box is a blunder.

words.meaning: To look at something very closely to find any problem.
words.example: Gobber scrutinized every dragon in the training ring.

words.meaning: Done on purpose, after careful thinking.
words.example: Choosing the area model was a deliberate choice, not a guess.

words.meaning: Proud and happy after winning or succeeding.
words.example: The tribe gave a triumphant cheer when the danger was over.

slides.title: Pick the tool, then scrutinize
slides.text: 🧠 Fact: both numbers 10 or less. 🔧 Break apart: a teen or a tens number. 📐 Area model: bigger numbers.

visual.sub: 17 is a teen number: break it apart in your head

slides.tip: Four blunders to scrutinize for: lost zero, wrong fact, missing box, lost count.

slides.title: Pick the tool
slides.text: Type fact, break apart or area model.

items.q: Which tool is optimal for 8 × 7?
items.why: Both numbers are 10 or less: just know it. 8 × 7 = 56.

items.q: Which tool is optimal for 53 × 28?
items.why: Both numbers have two digits and neither is a teen or tens number: area model with four boxes.
items.no: Is 53 a teen or a tens number?

items.q: Break apart in your head: 17 × 8 = ____
items.no: Split 17 into 10 + 7. Multiply each part by 8, then add.

slides.title: Fix the blunder
slides.text: Scrutinize the work. Type the right answer.

items.q: Snotlout wrote 35 × 8 = 24 + 40 = 64. Fix the blunder. What is 35 × 8?
Fishlegs wrote 24 × 15 = 200 + 20 = 220. What is 24 × 15 really?
Gobber added 8 again and again for 13 × 8 and got 96. How many 8s did he really add?

slides.title: Two-step problems
slides.text: Plan first: what do you do first, and what next? Type just the number.

items.q: Stoick has 600 coins. He buys 7 helmets that cost 68 coins each. How many coins are left?
There are 5 nests with 23 eggs each and 3 nests with 17 eggs each. How many eggs in all?
items.no: Multiply for each kind of nest, then add.

items.q: Estimate: 58 × 22 is between 1,000 and ____.
Which partial products build 87 × 9?
no: 80 × 9 is 8 tens × 9 = 72 tens = 720.
The 7 box gets multiplied too: 7 × 9 = 63.
Those are the parts of 87. Multiply each one by 9.

slides.title: Use your words
slides.text: Type the word from memory.

items.q: Gobber looked very closely at every box to find mistakes. He ________ the work.
items.why: To scrutinize is to look very closely to find any problem.
items.no: Which word means to look very closely for problems?

items.q: Writing 7 × 8 = 54 is a careless mistake. A careless mistake is a ________.
items.no: Which word means a careless mistake?

items.q: Which choice is deliberate?
choices: Hiccup plans his words carefully before he speaks to the dragon.
Hiccup sneezes in the middle of a speech.
items.why: Deliberate means done on purpose, after careful thinking.
no: Tripping is an accident, not on purpose.
A sneeze is not planned.

sets.q: What is the optimal way to find 16 × 9?
choices: Just know it as a basic fact
no: Correct but slow, and easy to lose count.
9 has only one digit, so there are not four boxes.
16 × 9 is bigger than the basic facts.

sets.q: Which problem should you solve with an area model on paper?
no: A basic fact: just know it.
One fact and a zero: 240.
Break apart in your head: 70 + 7.

sets.q: What is 367 × 8?
What is 29 × 16?
Gobber wrote 85 × 7 = 560 + 35 = 595. Is his work valid? Type valid or not valid.
sets.why: 80 × 7 = 560 and 5 × 7 = 35. Every box is right, so it is valid.

sets.q: Snotlout wrote 47 × 6 = 240 + 46 = 286. Fix the blunder. What is 47 × 6?
A Viking ship makes 18 trips. Each trip carries 25 sheep. How many sheep?
sets.no: 18 equal trips of 25. Use four boxes.

sets.q: Hiccup reads 45 pages a day for 6 days. His book has 300 pages. How many pages are left?
To scrutinize an area model means to …
choices: draw it as fast as you can
look at every box very closely for mistakes
sets.why: Scrutinize means to look very closely.
no: Scrutinize is slow and careful.
That would make a blunder.
Scrutinize means checking it yourself.

sets.q: Fishlegs rushed and forgot to multiply the ones box. That careless mistake was a ______ in his work.
sets.why: A blunder is a careless mistake.
no: A method is a way of doing something, not a mistake.
Deliberate means on purpose. This was careless.
Triumphant means proud after winning.

sets.q: What is the optimal way to find 18 × 7?
choices: Just know it as a basic fact
no: 18 × 7 is bigger than the basic facts.
Correct but slow, and easy to lose count.
18 has only two digits, so three boxes makes no sense.

sets.q: Which problem can you just know as a basic fact?
no: 16 is bigger than 10. Break it apart.
Both numbers are too big for a basic fact.
69 needs two boxes.

sets.q: What is 485 × 6?
What is 38 × 26?
Fishlegs wrote 63 × 9 = 540 + 27 = 567. Is his work valid? Type valid or not valid.
sets.why: 60 × 9 = 540 and 3 × 9 = 27. Every box is right, so it is valid.

sets.q: Gobber wrote 74 × 8 = 56 + 32 = 88. Fix the blunder. What is 74 × 8?
Each of 14 dragons eats 35 fish. How many fish?
sets.no: 14 equal groups of 35. Use four boxes.

sets.q: Hiccup has 400 coins. He buys 9 maps that cost 36 coins each. How many coins are left?
Which moment would make Hiccup feel triumphant?
choices: losing his helmet in the sea
finally training his dragon after many tries
sets.why: Triumphant means proud and happy after winning or succeeding.
no: That would make him upset, not proud.
Waiting is not winning.
That is embarrassing, not triumphant.

sets.q: A method is …
choices: a way of doing something, step by step
sets.why: A method is a way of doing something, step by step.
no: That is a blunder.
That is optimal.
That is triumphant.

sets.q: What is the optimal way to find 14 × 8?
choices: Just know it as a basic fact
no: Correct but slow, and easy to lose count.
8 has only one digit, so there are not four boxes.
14 × 8 is bigger than the basic facts.

sets.q: Which problem needs an area model on paper?
sets.why: Two 2-digit numbers need four boxes on paper.
no: A basic fact: just know it (48).
One fact and a zero: 210.
Break apart in your head: 60 + 12 = 72.

sets.q: What is 629 × 7?
What is 43 × 27?
Snotlout wrote 64 × 6 = 360 + 34 = 394. Is his work valid? Type valid or not valid.
sets.why: 4 × 6 is 24, not 34. The right answer is 384, so his work is not valid.

sets.q: Fishlegs wrote 26 × 17 = 200 + 42 = 242. He left out two boxes. What is 26 × 17?
22 Vikings each carry 45 rocks. How many rocks?
sets.no: 22 equal groups of 45. Use four boxes.

sets.q: Gobber needs 500 nails. He has 9 bags with 47 nails each. How many more nails does he need?
Gobber wants to scrutinize Hiccup's work. What does he do?
choices: He looks at every step very closely for mistakes.
sets.why: Scrutinize means to look at something very closely to find any problem.
no: That is abandoning it, not scrutinizing it.
Scrutinizing is slow and careful.
Cheering is not checking.

sets.q: Which sentence uses valid correctly?
choices: I ate a valid sandwich for lunch.
Your answer is valid because each box is correct and it fits the estimate.
sets.why: Valid means correct and based on good reasons.
no: Valid describes reasoning or answers, not a dragon.
A sandwich is not correct or incorrect.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one. Only your first try counts. Pick the optimal method, then scrutinize your answer.

questions.q: Which problem can you just know as a basic fact?
no: 18 is bigger than 10. Break it apart.
Both numbers are too big for a basic fact.
89 needs boxes.

questions.q: Fishlegs wrote 91 × 7 = 630 + 7 = 637. Is his work valid? Type valid or not valid.
Hiccup wrote 58 × 7 = 350 + 54 = 404. Fix the blunder. What is 58 × 7?
Snotlout added 6 again and again for 16 × 6 and got 90. He lost count. What is 16 × 6 really?
The tribe has 7 boats with 36 rowers each and 4 boats with 18 rowers each. How many rowers in all?
questions.no: Multiply for each kind of boat, then add.

no: Too small: 40 × 20 is already 800.
Too big: 50 × 30 is only 1,500.

questions.q: A deliberate choice is one you make …
questions.why: Deliberate means done on purpose, after careful thought.
no: That is the opposite of deliberate.
Deliberate is about thinking, not sound.
Deliberate means you thought about it.

choices: My method for ×9 facts is ×10 minus one group.
A method is a mistake you find in someone's work.
questions.why: A method is a way of doing something.
no: 42 is the answer, not the method.
That is a blunder.

questions.q: Which word means the best possible choice for the job?
questions.why: Optimal means the best possible choice for the job.
no: A blunder is a careless mistake.
Valid means correct and based on good reasons.
Deliberate means done on purpose, after thinking.

teacher.objective: Bailey chooses the optimal method for a multiplication problem (basic fact, break apart in her head, or area model on paper), finds and fixes blunders in someone else's repeated adding or area model, and solves one- and two-step word problems. This is the Prove it lesson for the area model week.
materials: The Class Lesson on a laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Index cards: 8 problems for the hands-on tool sort (9 × 8, 7 × 7, 14 × 6, 60 × 8, 12 × 9, 57 × 6, 426 × 7, 32 × 16)
Three paper plates or sticky notes labeled 🧠 Fact, 🔧 Break apart, 📐 Area model
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Her Lesson 7 packet page 1 (and the Lesson 6 packet) to check together

plan.do: Class slide 1. Check which of Tuesday's tasks are done. She names a tool for 9 × 7 and for 245 × 6.
Class slide 2. Push her to back up her opinion about Hiccup's choice with a detail from the book.
Class slide 3. Flip all 7 cards; she explains method vs. blunder.
Class slide 4. Check Lesson 7 packet page 1 (386 × 4 = 1,544) together, then 214 × 6 and 31 × 18 on the whiteboard.
Class slide 5. Fact / Break apart / Area model columns on the whiteboard.
Class slide 6. She sorts your 8 index cards onto the 3 plates, says why for each, and solves one card from each plate.
Class slides 7–8. She names the tool out loud before every tap.
Class slide 9. She names each of the four blunders in her own words.
Class slide 10. 53 × 8 = 40 + 24 = 64 on the whiteboard; she estimates, circles the lost zero in red and fixes it (424).
Class slide 11. She names the type of blunder before tapping.
Class slide 12. Quick and out loud.
Class slides 13–14. She underlines the question and writes the plan (multiply, then subtract or compare) before computing.
Class slide 15. Quick and out loud.
Class slide 16 on her own: pick the tool for 14 × 7 and fix 47 × 8. No hints.
Class slide 17. Celebrate the week. Read the weekend task list together, including Multiplication Mountain Lesson 1.

watch: Choosing the area model for everything, even 9 × 7. Say: the optimal tool is the fastest one that still gets it right.
Defaulting back to adding over and over when a number feels big. Ask: how many boxes would this need? Then draw them.
Saying "there is no blunder" without checking. Make her redo one box and compare it to the estimate before deciding.
In two-step problems, stopping after the multiplication (192 oars instead of 42). Have her reread the question sentence and underline what it asks.
"I can't do it" on 29 × 16. Point to the four boxes: each one is a fact she knows.

packet_key.answer: Any sentence that uses deliberate to mean on purpose, after thinking (for example, I made a deliberate choice to draw an area model).
Two complete sentences that answer yes or no and give one detail from the book as proof.

teacher.notes: This weekend she does the After-Class Lesson on her own; it ends with Show What You Know (3 different sets for retakes; she needs 90 to open Lesson 9). Lesson 9 (Monday, on Zoom) starts division. If she scores under 90, do not move on yet: on Monday, spend the first 10 minutes on two-box and four-box models and one blunder hunt, then let her retake this check (she gets a new set). If her misses are word problems, have her say the plan (multiply, then subtract) before solving.

slides.title: Pick the Smartest Method
slides.text: You have three tools now: facts, break apart, and the area model. Today you prove you can pick the right tool and catch a blunder in someone else's work.

notes.do: Before class: check her Lesson 7 score (Formspree) and whether Lesson 6's practice and packet, Lesson 7's practice and Lesson 7 packet page 1 are done. Lay out the 8 index cards, 3 labeled plates, red pencil, whiteboard and grid paper.
notes.say: This week you learned two big tools: break apart and the area model. Today is Prove it. You pick the best tool, and you catch other people's blunders.
notes.ask: Which tool would you use for 9 × 7? For 245 × 6?
notes.listen: 9 × 7: just know it (63). 245 × 6: area model with three boxes. If she says area model for 9 × 7, that is today's big lesson.

slides.title: Choices and results
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: What is the most exciting thing that has happened so far? Tell it with details.
Find a choice Hiccup made. Was it a deliberate choice or a quick guess? Use a detail to explain.
If you could give Hiccup one piece of advice right now, what would it be, and why?
starters: Hiccup chose to … I think it was …
I would tell Hiccup to … because …

notes.do: 5–6 minutes. Push for a detail from the book to back up every opinion. Tap the gold star for proof from the text.
notes.ask: Was Hiccup's choice deliberate or a quick guess? How do you know? What advice would you give him?
notes.listen: A strong answer quotes or retells a specific event. Link it: in math, picking a method should also be deliberate, not a quick grab for the longest way.

words.meaning: Correct and based on good reasons.

Writing 42 instead of 420 in the 60 box is a blunder.

words.meaning: To look at something very closely to find any problem.

notes.do: She flips all 7 cards and reads them aloud.
notes.say: Optimal, valid, blunder and scrutinize are the words a math checker uses. Deliberate and triumphant are great words for your book.

notes.do: Look at her Lesson 7 packet page 1 together (item 9: 386 × 4 = 1,544). Then she does these two on the whiteboard.
notes.ask: How many boxes does each one need? What is your estimate first?
notes.listen: 1,284 and 558. If she gets 308 for 31 × 18, she did only two boxes (300 + 8): have her count four.

slides.title: Three tools: which one?
slides.text: Before you start, ask: Which method is optimal?

steps.text: 🧠 Know the fact. Both numbers are 10 or less. 9 × 7 = 63. Done!
🔧 Break apart in your head. One number is a teen (11–19) or a tens number. 12 × 8 = 80 + 16 = 96.
📐 Area model on paper. Bigger numbers: 68 × 7, 245 × 6, 23 × 14.
🐢 Adding over and over is never optimal for big numbers. It is slow and easy to lose count.

slides.tip: Ask yourself: Do I know it? Can I split it in my head? If not, draw the boxes.

notes.do: Click the steps one at a time. Draw three columns on the whiteboard: 🧠 Fact, 🔧 Break apart, 📐 Area model.
notes.say: The optimal tool is the fastest one that still gets it right. Big tools for big numbers. Small tools for small numbers.
notes.ask: Why is adding over and over never optimal for big numbers? When would you break apart in your head?
notes.listen: Too slow and easy to lose count. Break apart when one number is a teen (11–19) or a tens number.

slides.title: Sort the cards
slides.text: Your teacher has 8 cards and 3 plates: 🧠 Fact, 🔧 Break apart, 📐 Area model.

steps.text: Put each card on a plate. Say why out loud.
Pick one card from each plate and solve it on the whiteboard.
Was each tool the optimal one? Would a different tool be faster?

slides.tip: Ask: Do I know it? Can I split it in my head? If not, draw the boxes.

notes.do: Cards: 9 × 8, 7 × 7, 14 × 6, 60 × 8, 12 × 9, 57 × 6, 426 × 7, 32 × 16. She sorts all 8 onto the plates, then solves one card from each plate (for example 7 × 7 = 49, 14 × 6 = 60 + 24 = 84, 32 × 16 = 300 + 20 + 180 + 12 = 512).
notes.say: Tell me why each card goes on its plate. 'Because it is big' is not enough: tell me what kind of number it is.
notes.ask: Why does 60 × 8 go on Break apart and not Area model? Why does 57 × 6 need paper?
notes.listen: 60 × 8 is one fact and a zero (480). 57 × 6 is not a teen or a tens number, so two boxes on paper (300 + 42 = 342). Accept 12 × 9 on Break apart (90 + 18 = 108).

slides.title: Pick the tool
slides.text: Tap a problem, then tap the tool you would use.

items.why: 5 × 9 = 45, so 450. One fact and a zero.

items.hint: 78 is not a teen or a tens number.

slides.done: Facts for small numbers, break apart for teens and tens, area model for the big ones.

notes.do: Now the same sort on screen. She says the reason before each tap.
notes.ask: Is 11 × 6 a fact or a break apart? Why?
notes.listen: Break apart: 11 = 10 + 1, so 60 + 6 = 66. 78 × 9 is an area model because 78 is not a teen or a tens number.

items.q: What is the optimal way to find 19 × 6?
items.why: 19 sixes is one six less than 20 sixes: 120 − 6 = 114.
no: That works but it is slow. 19 is close to 20, so use a shortcut.
19 has only two digits. Three boxes makes no sense here.
The 9 must be multiplied by 6 too: 9 × 6 = 54.

items.q: Hiccup wants to find 238 × 7. Which method makes sense?
choices: Just know it as a fact
no: Far too slow, and easy to lose count.
238 × 7 is not a basic fact.
That is adding, not multiplying.

items.q: So what is 238 × 7?
no: You added 238 + 7.
You left out the ones box: 8 × 7 = 56.

notes.do: She names the tool out loud before she taps anything.
notes.ask: 19 is close to which tens number? How does that help?
notes.listen: 19 is one less than 20, so 20 × 6 − 6 = 114. For 238 × 7, three boxes: 1,400 + 210 + 56 = 1,666.

slides.title: Spot the blunder
slides.text: Good mathematicians scrutinize work. Here are four blunders to watch for.

steps.text:
Blunder 1: the lost zero. 62 × 7 = 42 + 14 = 56 ❌
The 60 box is 60 × 7 = 420, not 42. Fixed: 420 + 14 = 434.

Blunder 3: the missing box. 25 × 13 = 200 + 15 = 215 ❌
There are four boxes. Fixed: 200 + 50 + 60 + 15 = 325.

steps.text:
Blunder 4: lost count. Snotlout added 9 again and again for 12 × 9 and got 99 ❌
99 is only eleven 9s. Fixed: 90 + 18 = 108.

slides.tip: Your estimate catches blunders. 62 × 7 must be between 60 × 7 = 420 and 70 × 7 = 490, so 56 cannot be right.

notes.do: Click one blunder at a time. Before she reads the fix line, she says in her own words what went wrong.
notes.say: Good mathematicians scrutinize. There are four blunders that show up again and again: the lost zero, the wrong fact, the missing box and lost count.
notes.ask: How would an estimate have caught Blunder 1? Which blunder do YOU make most?
notes.listen: 62 × 7 must be between 420 and 490, so 56 cannot be right. Honest answers are good: use her answer as her personal watch-for.

slides.title: Red pencil blunder hunt
slides.text: Your teacher writes this on the whiteboard. Scrutinize it with a red pencil.

steps.text: Estimate: 50 × 8 = 400. So 64 is far too small.
The 50 box is 50 × 8 = 400, not 40. That is a lost zero.

slides.tip: Always check with an estimate first. It tells you a blunder is hiding.

notes.do: Write 53 × 8 = 40 + 24 = 64 on the whiteboard BEFORE showing the steps. Hand her the red pencil. She circles the blunder and writes the fix. Then click through the steps to confirm.
notes.say: You are the checker. Do not redo it from scratch; scrutinize each box.
notes.ask: Before you look at any box: is 64 a reasonable answer? Which box is wrong? What kind of blunder is it?
notes.listen: Not reasonable (should be about 400). The 50 box: lost zero. 424. If she says 'he should add 53 + 8', ask: what does the × sign mean?

items.q: Snotlout found 83 × 9 like this: 72 + 27 = 99. What is the blunder?
choices: He used the wrong fact. 3 × 9 is 24.
There is no blunder. 99 is correct.
He lost the zero. 80 × 9 = 720, so the answer is 747.
no: 3 × 9 really is 27. Look at the 80 box.
83 × 9 must be more than 80 × 9 = 720, so 99 is far too small.
The sign says multiply.

items.q: Fishlegs added 7 again and again for 15 × 7 and got 98. What happened?
choices: He added one 7 too many. The answer is 91.
There is no blunder. 98 is correct.
no: 98 is fourteen 7s, so he added one too few, not too many.

items.q: This area model for 36 × 24 has one blunder. Which box is wrong?

no: 3 × 2 = 6, and two zeros make 600. Correct.
3 × 4 = 12, then one zero: 120. Correct.
That fact is right.

notes.do: She names the type of blunder (lost zero, wrong fact, missing box, lost count) before tapping.
notes.ask: What type of blunder is this? How would you prove it?
notes.listen: 83 × 9: lost zero (747). 15 × 7: lost count, only fourteen 7s (105). 36 × 24: the 6 × 20 box lost its zero (120, total 864).

items.q: What is 92 × 8?
no: You added 92 + 8.
The ones box is 2 × 8 = 16, not 2.

items.q: Which is the best estimate for 21 × 38?
no: Too many zeros.

items.q: Which four partial products build 41 × 17?
no: Only two boxes. You need all four.
Keep the zeros: 40 × 10 = 400 and 40 × 7 = 280.

notes.ask: What is your estimate for 21 × 38? How many partial products does 41 × 17 have?

slides.title: Two-step problems: plan first
slides.text: Gobber has 500 nails. He uses 7 bags with 38 nails in each bag. How many nails are left?

steps.text: Plan: First multiply to find the nails he used. Then subtract from 500.
Step 2. 500 − 266 = 234 nails left.
Check: did you answer the question? It asks how many are left, so 234, not 266.

slides.tip: Underline the question. Words like left, more, in all and difference tell you the second step.

notes.do: Click the steps. Before step 1, she underlines the question on the whiteboard copy and says the plan in her own words.
notes.say: Two-step problems are where people stop too early. Plan both steps before you compute anything.
notes.ask: What is the question asking for? What do you do first? What is the second step?
notes.listen: Plan: multiply, then subtract. If she says 266 is the answer, ask her to read the last sentence again: how many are LEFT?

items.q: Each of 9 dragons eats 8 fish a day. How many fish do they eat in a week?
no: That is one day. A week has 7 days, so do 72 × 7.
You added 9 + 8 + 7.
72 × 7 = 490 + 14. Check the ones box.

items.q: Stoick has 12 ships. Each ship needs 16 oars. He already has 150 oars. How many more oars does he need?
no: That is all the oars he needs. He already has 150, so subtract.
You added 150 more. He already has those oars, so subtract.

items.q: Fishlegs buys 3 books that cost 124 coins each. Hiccup buys 4 books that cost 95 coins each. Who spends more, and by how much?
no: Fishlegs spends 372 and Hiccup spends 380. Who has more?
29 is the difference in one book's price. Compare the totals.
372 and 380 are not the same.

notes.do: For each problem she writes the plan (multiply, then subtract / compare / multiply again) before computing.
notes.ask: What is the plan? Which number is the answer to the question, not just the first step?
notes.listen: Dragons: 72 a day, then × 7 = 504. Oars: 192 needed − 150 = 42. Books: 372 and 380, Hiccup by 8.

items.q: The optimal method for a problem is …
choices: the best possible choice for that job
the longest method, so you are careful
items.why: Optimal means the best possible choice.
no: For 9 × 7 the area model is not the best choice.
Long is not the same as best.
Optimal depends on the problem, not on a friend.

items.q: Which sentence uses valid correctly?
choices: The dragon gave a valid roar and flew away.
I was so valid that I ate three fish.
Her answer is valid because every partial product is correct.
items.why: Valid means correct and based on good reasons.
no: Valid means correct and well-reasoned. A roar is not correct or incorrect.
Valid does not describe hunger or feelings.

items.q: When the danger was over, the Vikings gave a triumphant cheer. How did they feel?
choices: scared that it would come back
proud and happy because they succeeded
items.why: Triumphant means proud and happy after winning.
no: That is fear, not triumph.
A triumphant cheer is full of energy.
Triumphant people know they won.

notes.do: She reads every choice and says why each wrong one is wrong.
notes.ask: Why is 'always the area model' not what optimal means?
notes.listen: Optimal depends on the problem; for 9 × 7 the fact is optimal. Valid = correct with good reasons. Triumphant = proud after winning.

slides.title: Check for understanding
slides.text: On your own. No help this time.

items.q: Which tool is optimal for 14 × 7? Type fact, break apart or area model.
items.why: 14 is a teen number: 70 + 28 = 98 in your head. Break apart is optimal.
items.no: Is 14 a teen number or a tens number?

items.q: Snotlout wrote 47 × 8 = 320 + 54 = 374. Fix the blunder. What is 47 × 8?

notes.do: She works alone. You watch only.
notes.say: Show me you can pick the tool and catch a blunder by yourself.
notes.listen: Break apart, and 376 (wrong fact). If she types area model, accept her reason aloud but remind her the optimal tool is the fastest one that still works.

slides.title: A triumphant week
slides.text: On Monday you saw why adding 8 seventy-five times is slow. Today you pick the smartest tool and catch blunders.

steps.text: 🧠 Know the fact for small numbers.
🔧 Break apart in your head for teens and tens.
📐 Area model on paper for big numbers. Estimate first, count your boxes.
🔍 Scrutinize: lost zero, wrong fact, missing box, lost count.

slides.tip: Weekend work: after-class lesson, practice, packet, Lesson 7 packet page 2, Multiplication Mountain and reading.

notes.do: Click through the steps. Open the course page and read the weekend task list together, including Multiplication Mountain Lesson 1.
notes.say: You did it. On Monday you raced to add 8s, and it was slow. Today you chose the optimal tool and found other people's blunders. That is a triumphant week.
notes.ask: Which tool do you feel strongest with now? Which blunder will you watch for?
notes.listen: Any honest answer. Write her watch-for blunder on a sticky note for her packet.
